title: Lippan Kaam: How Gujarat’s Ancient Mud-and-Mirror Craft Is Transforming Modern Homes
excerpt: Once confined to the circular huts of Kutch, the centuries-old art of lippan — mixing clay, camel dung, and mirrors into shimmering wall panels — is finding a new audience among urban homeowners and interior designers worldwide.
body:
• Lippan kaam, a centuries-old mud-and-mirror wall art from Gujarat’s Kutch region, is experiencing a revival as interior designers incorporate it into luxury urban homes.
  • The craft involves shaping a clay-and-dung mixture into raised patterns on walls and embedding cut mirrors to create shimmering, light-reflective surfaces.
  • Originally practised by women artisans to decorate bhungas (circular mud huts), lippan art now commands premium prices on global platforms and has become a sought-after element in high-end residential design.

Walk into a traditional bhunga — one of the circular mud huts that dot the Kutch landscape in Gujarat — and your eyes are immediately drawn to the walls. Raised patterns of clay, studded with small mirrors, catch whatever light enters the doorway and scatter it across the room in fractured gleams. This is lippan kaam, a decorative art form that has adorned the homes of Kutch’s pastoral communities for centuries. And increasingly, it is showing up in places its original practitioners could scarcely have imagined: luxury apartments in Mumbai, designer showrooms in Delhi, and curated home decor collections shipped to buyers in the United States and Europe.

Roots in the Desert

Lippan art has its origins in the Rabari, Ahir, and other pastoral communities of Kutch, where women traditionally decorated the interiors of their homes as both creative expression and practical insulation. The word “lippan” itself derives from “lipai,” meaning to plaster or coat. The base material — called matti — is a mixture of locally sourced clay and camel or horse dung, kneaded with water into a workable dough.

Artisans roll the dough into thin coils, press them onto walls, and shape them into geometric patterns, floral motifs, or depictions of animals and daily life. Small pieces of mirror are then embedded into the wet surface. Once dry, a coat of white clay gives the finished work its distinctive pale backdrop, against which the mirrors throw light in every direction.

“The plain or colourful mud and camel dung plaster does not only add a decorative touch but also helps insulate the hut, keeping it cool in summer.”

— Dilip Abnave, Indian Traditional and Tribal Arts

From Village Walls to Urban Interiors

The transition from folk craft to luxury design element has been gradual but accelerating. Interior designers working with clients who want spaces that feel “deeply Indian, not in ornamentation, but in spirit,” as one Hyderabad-based architect put it, have found lippan panels to be a versatile solution. They work as accent walls in living rooms, statement pieces in entryways, or textural backdrops in meditation spaces.

The craft’s appeal lies partly in its tactile quality — the raised clay patterns invite touch in a way that printed wallpaper or painted surfaces cannot. The mirror inlays add a functional dimension as well, amplifying natural light in dim interiors and creating visual depth that shifts throughout the day.

A Global Market

Platforms like Etsy have become significant distribution channels for lippan art. Artisans and small studios now offer ready-to-hang panels on MDF boards, making the craft accessible to buyers who may not have mud walls to plaster. Prices range from under $50 for small mandala designs to several hundred dollars for large custom commissions. Studios in Bangalore, Ahmedabad, and even San Ramon, California, ship lippan pieces worldwide.

The adaptation to modern materials — air-dry clay replacing the traditional dung mixture, MDF boards substituting for mud walls — has drawn some criticism from purists. But proponents argue that the core technique and aesthetic remain intact, and that the commercial market provides livelihoods for artisans who might otherwise abandon the craft.

Cultural Significance

Within Kutch’s communities, lippan kaam has always been more than decoration. The mirror motifs often echo the embroidery patterns found on the clothing worn by women of the community, creating a visual language that connects textiles, architecture, and identity. Among Muslim artisans in the region, the art form traditionally favours geometric and abstract patterns, producing work that is both culturally specific and visually striking.

For diaspora families, a lippan panel on a living room wall can serve as a quiet assertion of heritage — less obvious than a prayer corner, more personal than a mass-produced print. It is a piece of the desert, shaped by hand, catching the light in a new country.
